reference_drawer.title: 📖 Prime Divisibility & Theorem Guide
reference_drawer.description: Essential rules and theorems for the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic:

items.rule: Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.
Let p be a prime number. If p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.
items.example: If 2 divides p², then 2 divides p.

items.rule: Sum of all digits is a multiple of 3
Double the last digit and subtract from remaining number; result is divisible by 7
Difference between sum of alternate digits is 0 or a multiple of 11
For a number to end with the digit 0, its prime factorisation must contain BOTH 2 and 5 (since 10 = 2 × 5).
items.example: 6ⁿ = (2 × 3)ⁿ lacks prime 5, so cannot end in 0.

concepts.title: Theorem 1.1: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
concepts.statement: Every composite number can be uniquely expressed as a product of prime powers.
concepts.explanation: Apart from the order of factors, the prime factorisation of any positive integer is strictly unique.
notes: Factors are written in ascending order: 2, 3, 5...
Uniqueness guarantees no other prime factors exist.

concepts.title: Prime vs. Composite Numbers
concepts.statement:
• Prime: Exactly 2 factors (1 and itself).
• Composite: More than 2 factors.
notes: 2 is the only even prime number.

concepts.title: Numbers Ending with Digit 0
concepts.statement: A number ends in 0 only if its prime base contains BOTH 2 and 5 (since 10 = 2 × 5).
concepts.explanation: For 6ⁿ = (2 × 3)ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ: only primes 2 and 3 exist. Since prime 5 is absent, 6ⁿ can never end in 0.
notes: Without prime factor 5, ending in 0 is impossible.

concepts.title: Theorem 1.2: Divisibility of Squares
concepts.statement: If prime p divides a², then p must also divide a.
concepts.explanation: Essential foundation for proving irrationality of √2, √3, √5.
notes: Applies only when p is a prime number.

worked_examples.title: Type 2: Proving Composite Numbers
worked_examples.problem: Explain why 5 × 11 × 13 + 13 is a composite number.

steps.statement: Factor out common term 13 using distributive property:

worked_examples.conclusion:
Since the given expression factors into $2^3 \times 7 \times 13$, it has factors other than 1 and itself (such as 13 and 56).

By the **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic**, every number with more than two factors is composite.

worked_examples.title: Type 3: Numbers Ending with Digit 0
worked_examples.problem: Check whether 15ⁿ can end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.

steps.statement: State the necessary condition for a number to end in digit 0:

steps.calculation: 2 \notin \{3, 5\} \implies 2 \text{ is not a prime factor of } 15^n

worked_examples.conclusion:
The only prime factors of $15^n$ are $3$ and $5$. By the uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, prime $2$ does not occur in the prime factorisation of $15^n$.

Without prime factor $2$, $15^n$ cannot be divisible by $10$.

**Therefore, $15^n$ cannot end with the digit 0 for any natural number $n$.**
worked_examples.final_answer: 15ⁿ cannot end with digit 0 because its prime factorisation 3ⁿ × 5ⁿ lacks the prime factor 2.
